a x^{2} + b x + c = a(x + b/(2a))^{2} +.title: Completing the square
a x^{2} + b x + c = a(x + b/(2a))^{2} +.about: Rewrites a quadratic as a perfect square plus a constant, which shows the vertex at once and is how the quadratic formula is derived.

r_{1} + r_{2} = −b/a, r_{1} r_{2} = c/a.title: Vieta's formulas: sum and product of the roots
r_{1} + r_{2} = −b/a, r_{1} r_{2} = c/a.about: For ax² + bx + c = 0 the two roots add to −b/a and multiply to c/a, real or complex. Handy for checking roots and for building a quadratic from its roots.
related: the monic quadratic with those roots

example.problem: Without solving, find the sum and product of the roots of 2x^{2} − 7x + 3 = 0.

p(x) = (x − r) q(x) + p(r).title: Remainder and factor theorems
p(x) = (x − r) q(x) + p(r).about: Dividing a polynomial by x − r leaves remainder p(r). So x − r is a factor exactly when p(r) = 0, which is how roots are tested and polynomials factored.

example.problem: Is x − 2 a factor of p(x) = x^{3} − 3x^{2} + 4?
steps: The remainder is 0, so x − 2 is a factor: p(x) = (x − 2)(x^{2} − x − 2)

log_{b}(x) = y ⇔ b^{y} = x.title: What a logarithm is
log_{b}(x) = y ⇔ b^{y} = x.about: log_b(x) is the exponent you raise b to in order to get x. Turning a log equation into exponent form (or back) is the first step in solving most of them.

log_{b}(x/y) = log_{b}(x) − log_{b}(y).title: Quotient rule for logarithms
log_{b}(x/y) = log_{b}(x) − log_{b}(y).about: The log of a quotient is the difference of the logs, because dividing powers of b subtracts their exponents.

y = a f(b(x − h)) + k.title: Transformations of a graph
y = a f(b(x − h)) + k.about: Starting from y = f(x): h shifts the graph right, k shifts it up, a stretches it vertically (and flips it if negative), and b squeezes it horizontally by 1/b (flipping it if negative).
vars: vertical stretch; a < 0 reflects in the x-axis
horizontal squeeze by 1/b; b < 0 reflects in the y-axis

example.problem: Describe y = −2(x − 3)^{2} + 1 starting from y = x^{2}.
example.answer: a downward parabola, vertex (3, 1), twice as steep

f(−x) = f(x).title: Even function
f(−x) = f(x).about: A function is even when replacing x by −x leaves it unchanged; its graph is a mirror image across the y-axis. Examples: x², cos(x), |x|.

f(−x) = −f(x).title: Odd function
f(−x) = −f(x).about: A function is odd when replacing x by −x flips its sign; its graph is unchanged by a half turn about the origin. Examples: x³, sin(x), tan(x). The integral of an odd function over [−a, a] is 0.

(f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x)).title: Composition of functions
(f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x)).about: Apply g first, then f to its result. Order matters: f(g(x)) is usually not g(f(x)).

example.problem: With f(x) = x^{2} and g(x) = x + 1, find (f ∘ g)(3) and (g ∘ f)(3).

f(f^{−1}(x)) = x.title: Inverse function
f(f^{−1}(x)) = x.about: The inverse undoes the function. To find it, write y = f(x), swap x and y, and solve for y. Its graph is the mirror image of f's across y = x; f must be one-to-one.

(f(x + h) − f(x))/h.title: Difference quotient: average rate of change
(f(x + h) − f(x))/h.about: The slope of the secant line from x to x + h: how fast f changes on average over a step h. As h shrinks to 0 it becomes the derivative f′(x).
assumptions: f defined at x and x + h
related: the same slope between two points

example.problem: Simplify the difference quotient of f(x) = x^{2}.
example.answer: 2x + h, which tends to 2x as h → 0

r^{2} = x^{2} + y^{2}.title: Polar radius from rectangular coordinates
r^{2} = x^{2} + y^{2}.about: A point (x, y) lies at distance r = √(x² + y²) from the origin, by Pythagoras. Pair it with θ = atan2(y, x) for the angle.

c^{2} = a^{2} − b^{2}.title: Foci of an ellipse
c^{2} = a^{2} − b^{2}.about: For x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 with a > b, the foci sit on the long axis at (±c, 0). Every point on the ellipse has distances to the two foci that add to 2a.

example.problem: Find the foci of x^{2}/25 + y^{2}/9 = 1.

c^{2} = a^{2} + b^{2}.title: Foci of a hyperbola
c^{2} = a^{2} + b^{2}.about: For x²/a² − y²/b² = 1 the foci are at (±c, 0) with c² = a² + b². Every point on the hyperbola has distances to the foci that differ by 2a.

example.problem: Find the foci of x^{2}/9 − y^{2}/16 = 1.

y = ±(b/a) x.title: Asymptotes of a hyperbola
y = ±(b/a) x.about: Far from the centre, x²/a² − y²/b² = 1 hugs the two lines y = ±(b/a)x. Sketch the box of half-width a and half-height b; its diagonals are the asymptotes.

example.problem: Give the asymptotes of x^{2}/4 − y^{2}/9 = 1.

x^{2} = 4 p y.title: Parabola opening up (focus and directrix)
x^{2} = 4 p y.about: Every point is equally far from the focus (0, p) and the directrix y = −p. Negative p opens down. Light from the focus reflects parallel to the axis, which is why dishes are parabolic.

example.problem: A dish follows x^{2} = 8y. Where is its focus?

e = c/a.title: Eccentricity of a conic
e = c/a.about: How stretched a conic is: 0 for a circle, between 0 and 1 for an ellipse, 1 for a parabola, more than 1 for a hyperbola. For an orbit it sets the shape of the ellipse.

example.problem: An ellipse has a = 5 and b = 3. Find e.

dT/dt = −k (T − T_{a}).title: Newton's law of cooling as an ODE
dT/dt = −k (T − T_{a}).about: A body's temperature changes at a rate proportional to its difference from the surroundings. The solution is T = T_{a} + (T_{0} − T_{a}) e^{−kt}.
assumptions: Ambient temperature constant; the body has one uniform temperature (lumped)

example.problem: Coffee at 90 °C sits in a 20 °C room with k = 0.05 /min. What is it after 10 min?

dy/dt + p y = q y^{n}.title: Bernoulli differential equation
dy/dt + p y = q y^{n}.about: A nonlinear first-order equation that the substitution v = y^{1−n} turns into a linear one: dv/dt + (1 − n) p v = (1 − n) q. Solve that with an integrating factor.
assumptions: n ≠ 0, 1 (for those it is already linear)

example.answer: y = 1/(1 + C e^{−t}), the logistic curve

M dx + N dy = 0.title: Exact equation
M dx + N dy = 0.about: If ∂M/∂y = ∂N/∂x, the left side is the total differential of some F(x, y). Find F from F_x = M and F_y = N; the solution is F(x, y) = C.

y′′ + 2ζω_{n} y′ + ω_{n}^{2} y = 0.title: Damped oscillator in standard form
y′′ + 2ζω_{n} y′ + ω_{n}^{2} y = 0.about: Dividing m y′′ + c y′ + k y = 0 by m. ζ < 1 oscillates (underdamped), ζ = 1 is critically damped, ζ > 1 creeps back (overdamped). The roots are r = −ζω_{n} ± ω_{n}√(ζ² − 1).

a t^{2} y′′ + b t y′ + c y = 0.title: Euler-Cauchy equation
a t^{2} y′′ + b t y′ + c y = 0.about: Each derivative is multiplied by the matching power of t, so y = t^{r} works. Distinct real r give t^{r₁} and t^{r₂}; a repeated r gives t^{r} and t^{r} ln t; complex α ± jβ give t^{α} cos(β ln t) and t^{α} sin(β ln t).

a r(r − 1) + b r + c = 0.title: Indicial equation of an Euler-Cauchy equation
a r(r − 1) + b r + c = 0.about: Putting y = t^{r} into a t² y″ + b t y′ + c y = 0 and dividing by t^{r} leaves this quadratic in r. Its roots give the solutions.

example.problem: Find r for t^{2} y″ + 3t y′ + y = 0.

y = y_{h} + y_{p}.title: General solution of a linear nonhomogeneous ODE
y = y_{h} + y_{p}.about: Every solution is the homogeneous solution (with its free constants) plus any one particular solution. Fit the constants to the initial conditions last, to the whole y.
vars: solves the equation with zero forcing
any one solution with the forcing

steps: y_{h} = c_{1} cos t + c_{2} sin t
example.answer: y = c_{1} cos t + c_{2} sin t + 2

y_{p} = −y_{1} ∫ y_{2} g/W dt + y_{2} ∫.title: Variation of parameters
y_{p} = −y_{1} ∫ y_{2} g/W dt + y_{2} ∫.about: A particular solution for any forcing g, built from two homogeneous solutions y₁, y₂ and their Wronskian. Use it when undetermined coefficients has no guess (tan t, 1/t, …).
assumptions: The equation is written with y″ having coefficient 1

example.problem: Find y_p for y″ + y = sec t.
steps: y_{1} = cos t, y_{2} = sin t, W = 1
y_{p} = −cos t ∫ tan t dt + sin t ∫ 1 dt
example.answer: y_p = cos t ln|cos t| + t sin t

t^{n} ‖ A_{n} t^{n} + … + A_{1} t + A_{0.title: Undetermined coefficients: polynomial forcing
t^{n} ‖ A_{n} t^{n} + … + A_{1} t + A_{0.about: For a polynomial forcing of degree n, guess a full polynomial of the same degree and match coefficients. Multiply by t if a constant already solves the homogeneous equation (c = 0).

example.problem: Find y_p for y″ + y = t^{2}.
steps: Guess A t^{2} + B t + C: 2A + A t^{2} + B t + C = t^{2}

e^{at} ‖ A e^{at}.title: Undetermined coefficients: exponential forcing
e^{at} ‖ A e^{at}.about: Exponential in, same exponential out. If a is a root of the characteristic equation, multiply the guess by t (by t² for a double root).

example.problem: Find y_p for y″ − y = e^{2t}.

cos(ωt), sin(ωt) ‖ A cos(ωt) + B sin(ωt).title: Undetermined coefficients: sinusoidal forcing
cos(ωt), sin(ωt) ‖ A cos(ωt) + B sin(ωt).about: Even if only a cosine drives the system, guess both cosine and sine, since damping shifts the phase. At resonance (jω a root) multiply by t.

example.problem: Find y_p for y″ + y′ = cos t.
steps: (−A + B) cos t + (−B − A) sin t = cos t

e^{at} cos(ωt) ‖ e^{at} (A cos(ωt) + B s.title: Undetermined coefficients: decaying or growing sinusoid
e^{at} cos(ωt) ‖ e^{at} (A cos(ωt) + B s.about: A product of exponential and sinusoid gets the same product as its guess, with both cosine and sine. Multiply by t if a ± jω is a characteristic root.

example.problem: Find y_p for y″ = e^{t} cos t.
steps: y″ of e^{t}(A cos t + B sin t) is e^{t}(2B cos t − 2A sin t)

cos(ω_{0}t), sin(ω_{0}t) ‖ t (A cos(ω_{0.title: Undetermined coefficients: resonance, times t
cos(ω_{0}t), sin(ω_{0}t) ‖ t (A cos(ω_{0.about: When the forcing is at the natural frequency, A cos(ω_{0}t) + B sin(ω_{0}t) already solves the homogeneous equation and can't be a particular solution. Multiply the guess by t; undamped, the response then grows linearly without bound.
assumptions: ±jω_{0} are roots of the characteristic equation (undamped, y″ + ω_{0}^{2} y = g)
If they are double roots, multiply by t^{2}
related: cos(ωt), sin(ωt) ‖ A cos(ωt) + B sin(ωt)

example.problem: Find y_p for y″ + y = cos t.
steps: cos t solves y″ + y = 0, so guess t (A cos t + B sin t)
y_p″ + y_p = 2B cos t − 2A sin t = cos t

x = c_{1} v_{1} e^{λ_{1}t} + c_{2} v_{2}.title: General solution of x′ = A x (distinct eigenvalues)
x = c_{1} v_{1} e^{λ_{1}t} + c_{2} v_{2}.about: Each eigenvalue and eigenvector give a solution that moves along that eigenvector; the general solution adds them. Negative real parts mean the motion decays to rest.

steps: λ = 2 with v = (1, 0); λ = −1 with v = (0, 1)

u = X(x) T(t).title: Separation of variables
u = X(x) T(t).about: Guess a product of one-variable functions. A PDE such as the heat equation then splits into two ODEs linked by a separation constant, and the boundary conditions pick the allowed modes, which add up as a Fourier series.

example.problem: Separate u_t = α u_{xx} with u = 0 at x = 0 and x = L.
steps: X T′ = α X″ T, so T′/(αT) = X″/X = −λ
example.answer: u = Σ b_{n} sin(nπx/L) e^{−α(nπ/L)^{2} t}

u = f(x − ct) + g(x + ct).title: d'Alembert's solution of the wave equation
u = f(x − ct) + g(x + ct).about: Any solution of the 1D wave equation is a shape moving right plus a shape moving left, both at speed c. With u(x, 0) = φ and u_t(x, 0) = 0, f = g = φ/2.

example.problem: A string starts at rest with shape φ(x). What is u?
example.answer: two half-height copies moving apart at speed c

c = (a + b)/2.title: Bisection method
c = (a + b)/2.about: If f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs, a root lies between. Test the midpoint c and keep the half where the sign still changes. Slow but it can't fail for a continuous f.
assumptions: f continuous on [a, b], f(a) f(b) < 0

example.problem: One step on f(x) = x^{2} − 2 over [1, 2].

x_{n+1} = g(x_{n}).title: Fixed-point iteration
x_{n+1} = g(x_{n}).about: Rewrite f(x) = 0 as x = g(x) and iterate. It converges near a fixed point where |g′| < 1, and faster the smaller |g′| is.

y = y_{0} + (y_{1} − y_{0})(x − x_{0})/(.title: Linear interpolation
y = y_{0} + (y_{1} − y_{0})(x − x_{0})/(.about: Reads a value between two table entries by assuming a straight line between them. Error is about h² f″/8 for spacing h.

example.problem: A steam table gives 2.0 at 100 and 2.6 at 120. Estimate at 105.

p(x) = Σ_{i=0}^{n} y_{i} Π_{j≠i} (x − x_.title: Lagrange interpolating polynomial
p(x) = Σ_{i=0}^{n} y_{i} Π_{j≠i} (x − x_.about: The one polynomial of degree ≤ n through n + 1 points. Each basis term is 1 at its own point and 0 at the others. High degrees on evenly spaced points can wiggle badly (Runge).

steps: p(x) = x^{2} + x + 1 fits all three

f′(x) ≈ (f(x) − f(x − h))/h.title: Backward difference
f′(x) ≈ (f(x) − f(x − h))/h.about: A one-sided slope using the point behind. First-order accurate, error ≈ (h/2) f″. Used when only past values exist, as in backward Euler.

∫ f dx ≈ h Σ_{i=0}^{n−1} f(x_{i} + h/2).title: Midpoint rule
∫ f dx ≈ h Σ_{i=0}^{n−1} f(x_{i} + h/2).about: Each strip uses f at its centre. Second-order accurate, with an error about half the trapezoid rule's and of opposite sign.

example.problem: Estimate ∫ x^{2} dx from 0 to 1 with the midpoint rule and n = 2.

E_{T} = −(b − a) h^{2} f′′(ξ)/12.title: Error of the composite trapezoid rule
E_{T} = −(b − a) h^{2} f′′(ξ)/12.about: The trapezoid rule's error shrinks with h²: halve the step and the error falls about 4 times. A convex f (f″ > 0) is overestimated.

example.problem: Bound the error for ∫ e^{x} dx on [0, 1] with h = 0.1.

y_{n+1} = y_{n} + h f(t_{n+1}, y_{n+1}).title: Backward (implicit) Euler
y_{n+1} = y_{n} + h f(t_{n+1}, y_{n+1}).about: Uses the slope at the end of the step, so y_{n+1} appears on both sides and must be solved for. First-order accurate but stable for stiff problems at any step size.

y_{n+1} = y_{n} + (h/2)(f(t_{n}, y_{n}).title: Heun's method (improved Euler)
y_{n+1} = y_{n} + (h/2)(f(t_{n}, y_{n}).about: Predict with an Euler step, then average the slopes at the start and at that predicted end. Second-order accurate; a two-stage Runge-Kutta method.

example.problem: y′ = y, y₀ = 1, h = 0.1. One step.

A = L U.title: LU decomposition
A = L U.about: Gaussian elimination stored as a lower-triangular L and upper-triangular U. Factor once, then solve each new right side cheaply by forward and back substitution. Partial pivoting (PA = LU) keeps it stable.

x_{i}^{(k+1)} = (b_{i} − Σ_{j≠i} a_{ij}.title: Jacobi iteration
x_{i}^{(k+1)} = (b_{i} − Σ_{j≠i} a_{ij}.about: Solve each equation for its own unknown, using the last guess for the others. Converges when A is diagonally dominant. Gauss-Seidel uses each new value at once and usually converges faster.

x_{k+1} = A x_{k}/‖A x_{k}‖.title: Power method
x_{k+1} = A x_{k}/‖A x_{k}‖.about: Repeated multiplication by A turns any start vector toward the eigenvector of the largest-magnitude eigenvalue. The Rayleigh quotient xᵀAx/xᵀx estimates that eigenvalue.

|e_{n+1}| ≈ C |e_{n}|^{p}.title: Order of convergence
|e_{n+1}| ≈ C |e_{n}|^{p}.about: How fast an iteration's error shrinks. p = 1 is linear (a fixed fraction each step, as bisection), p ≈ 1.618 is the secant method, p = 2 is quadratic (Newton: the correct digits double each step).

example.problem: Newton's errors go 10^{−2}, 10^{−4}, … What comes next?

log_{2}(n!) ≈ n log_{2}(n).title: Lower bound for comparison sorting
log_{2}(n!) ≈ n log_{2}(n).about: A comparison sort must tell apart all n! orderings, and each comparison gives one bit, so it needs at least log₂(n!) ≈ n log₂ n − 1.44 n comparisons. Merge sort and heapsort meet this bound.

example.problem: At least how many comparisons does sorting 1000 items take?

T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n) = Θ(n log n).title: Merge sort recurrence
T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n) = Θ(n log n).about: Split in half, sort both halves, merge in linear time. Each of the log₂ n levels does Θ(n) work: case 2 of the master theorem.

example.problem: About how many steps for n = 1,048,576 = 2^{20}?

T(n) = T(n/2) + Θ(1) = Θ(log n).title: Binary search recurrence
T(n) = T(n/2) + Θ(1) = Θ(log n).about: Each comparison halves a sorted range, so a search takes about log₂ n steps.

example.problem: Most comparisons to find a key among 1,000,000 sorted items?

E = 1/(1 − α).title: Expected probes in open addressing
E = 1/(1 − α).about: With uniform hashing, an unsuccessful search (or an insert) probes about 1/(1 − α) slots. It blows up as the table fills, which is why tables resize near α = 0.7.

n = 2^{h+1} − 1.title: Nodes in a perfect binary tree
n = 2^{h+1} − 1.about: Each level doubles: 1 + 2 + 4 + … + 2^{h}. So a balanced tree of n nodes has height about log₂ n.

example.problem: How many nodes does a perfect binary tree of height 9 hold?

E = V − 1.title: Edges in a tree
E = V − 1.about: A tree on V vertices, connected and without cycles, always has exactly V − 1 edges. Adding any edge makes a cycle; removing one disconnects it.

example.problem: A spanning tree of a 50-city network has how many links?

E = V(V − 1)/2.title: Edges in a complete graph
E = V(V − 1)/2.about: Every pair of vertices joined: V choose 2. That is the most a simple undirected graph can have, so a dense graph has Θ(V²) edges.

Σ deg(v) = 2E.title: Handshake lemma
Σ deg(v) = 2E.about: Each edge adds 1 to the degree of both its ends, so the degrees add to twice the edges. Hence the number of odd-degree vertices is even.

example.problem: 10 vertices each of degree 3. How many edges?

V − E + F = 2.title: Euler's formula for planar graphs
V − E + F = 2.about: A connected graph drawn in the plane without crossings has V − E + F = 2, counting the outer face. It gives E ≤ 3V − 6, so K₅ is not planar.

example.problem: A planar graph has 8 vertices and 12 edges. How many faces?

0 ≤ x ≤ 2^{n} − 1.title: Range of an unsigned integer
0 ≤ x ≤ 2^{n} − 1.about: n bits hold 2ⁿ values, from 0 up to 2ⁿ − 1. Going past the top wraps around to 0.

example.problem: Largest value of a 16-bit unsigned integer?

−2^{n−1} ≤ x ≤ 2^{n−1} − 1.title: Range of a two's complement integer
−2^{n−1} ≤ x ≤ 2^{n−1} − 1.about: Signed n-bit integers in two's complement give half the codes to negatives, so there is one more negative value than positive. Negate by flipping the bits and adding 1.

S = (1 − p) + p N.title: Gustafson's law
S = (1 − p) + p N.about: Speedup when the problem grows with the machine: with N processors and parallel fraction p of the run, the scaled speedup is close to N. A more hopeful view than Amdahl's fixed-size law.
vars: parallel fraction of the parallel run

L = λ W.title: Little's law
L = λ W.about: In a steady system, the average number inside equals the arrival rate times the average time each spends inside. It holds for any queue, store or server.

example.problem: A server gets 200 requests/s and each takes 50 ms. How many are in flight?

d = d_{proc} + d_{queue} + d_{trans} + d.title: Total delay at one network hop
d = d_{proc} + d_{queue} + d_{trans} + d.about: A packet waits for processing, for the queue, to be pushed onto the link (L/R) and to travel the link (d/s). Add them over the hops for end-to-end delay.

example.problem: 1500-byte packet on a 100 Mbit/s link of 2000 km (2 × 10^{8} m/s), no queue.

w = (X^{T} X + λI)^{−1} X^{T} y.title: Ridge regression, closed form
w = (X^{T} X + λI)^{−1} X^{T} y.about: Least squares with an L2 penalty λ‖w‖². Adding λI keeps XᵀX invertible and shrinks the weights, trading a little bias for less variance. Usually the intercept is not penalized.
vars: data matrix, one row per sample

ŷ = σ(w · x + b).title: Logistic regression
ŷ = σ(w · x + b).about: A linear score squashed by the sigmoid into a probability of the positive class. Trained by minimizing binary cross-entropy; the decision boundary w · x + b = 0 is a line or plane.

example.problem: w · x + b = 2. What is the predicted probability?

d(x, y) = √(Σ (x_{i} − y_{i})^{2}).title: Euclidean distance
d(x, y) = √(Σ (x_{i} − y_{i})^{2}).about: Straight-line distance between two feature vectors; what k-nearest neighbours and k-means use. Scale the features first, or the largest one dominates.

σ′(z) = σ(z)(1 − σ(z)).title: Derivative of the sigmoid
σ′(z) = σ(z)(1 − σ(z)).about: The sigmoid's slope comes from its own value, which makes backpropagation cheap. It peaks at 0.25 at z = 0 and vanishes for large |z|, the vanishing-gradient problem.

tanh(z) = (e^{z} − e^{−z})/(e^{z} + e^{−.title: Hyperbolic tangent activation
tanh(z) = (e^{z} − e^{−z})/(e^{z} + e^{−.about: An S-curve from −1 to 1, centred on 0, which often trains better than the sigmoid. tanh(z) = 2σ(2z) − 1, and its derivative is 1 − tanh².

A = softmax(Q K^{T}/√(d_{k})) V.title: Scaled dot-product attention
A = softmax(Q K^{T}/√(d_{k})) V.about: The core of transformers. Each query scores every key by dot product, scaled by √d_k so softmax stays soft; the softmax weights then average the values.

example.problem: One query q = (1, 0) and keys (1, 0), (0, 1), with d_k = 2. Find the weights.

RMSE = √(MSE).title: Root mean squared error
RMSE = √(MSE).about: The square root of the MSE, in the target's own units. It punishes large errors more than MAE does.

MAE = (1/n) Σ |y_{i} − ŷ_{i}|.title: Mean absolute error
MAE = (1/n) Σ |y_{i} − ŷ_{i}|.about: The average size of the errors, in the target's units. Less sensitive to outliers than MSE; minimizing it gives the median.

R^{2} = 1 − SS_{res}/SS_{tot}.title: Coefficient of determination (R squared)
R^{2} = 1 − SS_{res}/SS_{tot}.about: The share of the target's variance the model explains: 1 is perfect, 0 is no better than predicting the mean, and negative is worse. SS_res = Σ(yᵢ − ŷᵢ)², SS_tot = Σ(yᵢ − ȳ)².

L = −(y ln(ŷ) + (1 − y) ln(1 − ŷ)).title: Binary cross-entropy (log loss)
L = −(y ln(ŷ) + (1 − y) ln(1 − ŷ)).about: The loss for yes/no classifiers with a probability output. A confident wrong answer costs a lot; average it over the samples.

L = max(0, 1 − y ŷ).title: Hinge loss
L = max(0, 1 − y ŷ).about: The support vector machine's loss: zero once a sample is on the right side with margin 1, rising linearly otherwise.

example.problem: A sample has label y = 1. Find the hinge loss when the score ŷ is 2, 0.5 and −1.
steps: ŷ = 0.5: max(0, 1 − 0.5) = 0.5, right side but inside the margin

L + λ ‖w‖_{1}.title: L1 regularization (lasso)
L + λ ‖w‖_{1}.about: Adds the sum of absolute weights to the loss. Unlike L2 it drives many weights exactly to 0, which selects features.

G = 1 − Σ p_{i}^{2}.title: Gini impurity
G = 1 − Σ p_{i}^{2}.about: How mixed the classes at a decision-tree node are: 0 for a pure node, 0.5 at most for two classes. A split is chosen to lower the weighted impurity most.
vars: fraction of class i at the node

example.problem: A node is 70% class A and 30% class B.

IG = H(parent) − Σ (n_{k}/n) H(child_{k}.title: Information gain
IG = H(parent) − Σ (n_{k}/n) H(child_{k}.about: The fall in entropy from a split, the children weighted by size. ID3 and C4.5 trees split on the feature that gains most.

example.problem: A 50/50 parent (H = 1) splits into two pure halves.

v ← β v + ∇L, w ← w − η v.title: Gradient descent with momentum
v ← β v + ∇L, w ← w − η v.about: Keeps a running sum of past gradients, which speeds travel along consistent directions and damps zigzags. β ≈ 0.9 is typical.

example.problem: Gradient stays 1, β = 0.9. What does v tend to?

w ← w − η m̂/(√(v̂) + ϵ).title: Adam optimizer
w ← w − η m̂/(√(v̂) + ϵ).about: Keeps running averages of the gradient (m) and its square (v), corrects their start-up bias, and gives each weight its own step size. Defaults: η = 0.001, β₁ = 0.9, β₂ = 0.999, ϵ = 10⁻⁸.

example.problem: With m̂ = 0.2, v̂ = 0.04, η = 0.001, how far does w move?
example.answer: 0.001: Adam's steps are about η in size

x′ = (x − x_{min})/(x_{max} − x_{min}).title: Min-max normalization
x′ = (x − x_{min})/(x_{max} − x_{min}).about: Rescales a feature to [0, 1] using the training set's minimum and maximum. Sensitive to outliers; standardization is the alternative.

TNR = TN/(TN + FP).title: Specificity (true negative rate)
TNR = TN/(TN + FP).about: Of the real negatives, the share correctly called negative. Pairs with recall (sensitivity) in medical tests.

FPR = FP/(FP + TN).title: False positive rate
FPR = FP/(FP + TN).about: Of the real negatives, the share wrongly flagged: 1 − specificity. The ROC curve plots recall against FPR as the threshold moves; its area is the AUC.

EAR = (1 + r/n)^{n} − 1.title: Effective annual rate (APY)
EAR = (1 + r/n)^{n} − 1.about: What a quoted annual rate compounded n times a year really earns in a year. Compare loans and accounts by EAR, not APR.

FV = PV (1 + r)^{n}.title: Future value of a single sum
FV = PV (1 + r)^{n}.about: How much a sum grows to in n periods at rate r per period. The inverse of discounting.

PV = FV e^{−r t}.title: Continuous discounting
PV = FV e^{−r t}.about: Present value of a future amount when interest compounds continuously; the inverse of A = P e^{rt}.

B = P (1 + r)^{k} − M ((1 + r)^{k} − 1)/.title: Loan balance after k payments
B = P (1 + r)^{k} − M ((1 + r)^{k} − 1)/.about: What is still owed: the loan grown with interest, less the payments grown with interest. Early payments are mostly interest.

example.problem: $200,000 at 0.5% a month with M = $1199.10. Balance after 60 payments?

PV = C/r.title: Perpetuity
PV = C/r.about: Present value of a payment C every period forever. A preferred share or an endowment that pays only its interest.

PV = C/(r − g).title: Growing perpetuity (Gordon growth model)
PV = C/(r − g).about: Present value of payments that start at C next period and grow at g forever. As a stock price, P₀ = D₁/(r − g).

E[R] = r_{f} + β (E[R_{m}] − r_{f}).title: Capital asset pricing model (CAPM)
E[R] = r_{f} + β (E[R_{m}] − r_{f}).about: The return investors should expect from an asset: the risk-free rate plus β times the market risk premium. β measures how the asset moves with the market.

S = (R_{p} − r_{f})/σ_{p}.title: Sharpe ratio
S = (R_{p} − r_{f})/σ_{p}.about: Excess return per unit of risk (standard deviation). Higher is better when comparing portfolios.

WACC = (E/V) r_{E} + (D/V) r_{D} (1 − T).title: Weighted average cost of capital
WACC = (E/V) r_{E} + (D/V) r_{D} (1 − T).about: A firm's blended cost of money, the weights being market values of equity and debt. Interest is tax-deductible, hence (1 − T). Used as the discount rate for projects.
vars: equity and debt value, V = E + D

P = Σ_{t=1}^{n} C/(1 + y)^{t} + F/(1 + y.title: Bond price
P = Σ_{t=1}^{n} C/(1 + y)^{t} + F/(1 + y.about: The present value of the coupons and the face value at the yield. When yields rise, prices fall; a bond whose coupon rate equals its yield sells at par.

PM = (R − C)/R.title: Profit margin
PM = (R − C)/R.about: The share of each sale kept as profit.

D = (C − S)/n.title: Straight-line depreciation
D = (C − S)/n.about: Spreads an asset's cost, less what it can be sold for at the end, evenly over its life.
